newsitem.title: USA: Sun exec sees refiners hard hit by EPA plan.
newsitem.headline: Sun exec sees refiners hard hit by EPA plan.

text.p: A Sun Co Inc executive, adressing potential impacts of U.S. regulators' plans to change the definition of clean air, said oil refining is likely to be one of the hardest hit industrial sectors.

"Of all the business entities facing impacts from new (air quality) standards, the petroleum refining industry is among the most exposed," Thomas Wylie, Sun's vice president of government relations told executives attending the National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA) annual meeting.
"This is because we can expect new compliance pressures on both our refining processes and our products," Wylie said.

"The good news is that while our industry may be floundering in the deepest most dangerous parts of the regulatory pool, there are a lot of folks in the water with us," Wylie said. "It is clear that the...changes impact virtually every sector of the U.S. economy.
He noted that while estimates of total costs to U.S. industry are still being prepared, they are likely to soar into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
He said oil refiners will have to come up with new technologies to further control emissions from refineries themselves, as well as expand production of clean fuels.

If the proposal passes, Wylie said reformulated gasoline sales will have to spread well beyond their current areas in big cities like Los Angeles, Chicago and New York, just as even cleaner diesel fuels will have to expand.
He also noted the proposal, called the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), will spawn carpooling, enhanced vehicle emission inspection and maintenance and lower speed limits.

Wylie said U.S. industry, to convince the public the NAAQS proposal is excessive and onerous will use comments by the EPA's own independent science advisory board, the Clean Air Science Advisory Committee (CASAC).
He said CASAC has said the proposed ozone and particulate standards are not, or have not been linked to any appreciable health benefits, and that more studies must be done before either is adopted.

He said U.S. industry has adopted a three-pronged strategy to fight the plan including developing grass roots oppostion at the city, county and state level, bring that grass roots opposition to bear on the Washington, D.C. political in the hopes that Congress may force EPA to delay its proposal.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk, 1 212 859 1620
